name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Product Ops should auto-generate PR summaries from ticket diffs embedded in the release notes. This cuts manual copy-paste work and ensures engineers, marketers, and support see the same changes at once. The trade-off is trusting the auto-summary tool to capture nuance—so we’ll run a two-week pilot with human spot-checks before full rollout.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s live review gate fails when reviewers skip attendance—auto-summaries won’t fix the core problem. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a pre-review ticket diff checklist that engineers must complete before merging, shifting the burden from reviewers to engineers. Settle it by tracking merge delays before and after the change—if delays drop, the checklist wins.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory 48-hour async review window* for all PRs before merge, with auto-generated summaries from ticket diffs attached.

This forces engineers to submit complete, review-ready changes upfront, cutting the "live review gate" problem where reviewers skip attendance. The trade-off is slower merges when engineers rush to meet the window, but it shifts the burden from reviewers to the submitter—fixing the core failure mode.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 48-hour async window still lets engineers game the system by writing vague ticket diffs upfront, then dumping the real changes late—auto-summaries won’t catch what wasn’t there. Instead, Product Ops should require *pre-merge diffs to be attached to the PR* with a mandatory checklist of changed files, lines, and test coverage; settle it by tracking merge delays and rework rates before and after the change.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must require engineers to attach a *pre-merge diff* to every PR, with a mandatory checklist of changes tied to ticket IDs—no merge allowed until the diff matches the ticket’s scope.

Trade-off: Engineers lose flexibility to tweak changes last-minute, but we gain enforceable traceability and kill the "late dump" loophole. The artifact is the PR template with the diff field and checklist enforced in the merge gate.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s pre-merge diff rule solves the wrong problem: it turns engineers into bureaucrats without fixing the live review gate. The real risk is that last-minute tweaks—often the most critical fixes—get blocked by rigid diffs, forcing risky merges without live eyes. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *post-merge diff audit* within 24 hours, with auto-summaries attached to the release notes; this keeps the gate but shifts the burden to catching errors after, not before. Settle it by measuring how many critical fixes are caught in the audit vs. how many live reviews are skipped.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory 24-hour live review window* for all PRs with at least one reviewer assigned—no merge allowed until the session completes or the reviewer explicitly waives it.

Trade-off: This slows down merges slightly but forces real-time accountability, killing the "skip the gate" problem where reviewers dodge live sessions. Engineers lose the flexibility to merge quietly after async delays, but we gain visible, high-signal feedback loops.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 24-hour live window just shifts the problem: reviewers will still skip, now with a hard deadline. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory reviewer assignment* at PR creation—no merge until a reviewer is named and the PR is labeled "ready for review." Settle it by tracking merge delays tied to reviewer assignment failures.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must require *a single, named reviewer to explicitly accept responsibility for each PR* at creation—no merge allowed until that reviewer signs off or escalates.

This forces accountability upfront, not after delays or skipped reviews. Trade-off: Engineers must wait for a reviewer to commit, but we kill the "ghost reviewer" problem where PRs rot in limbo.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s named reviewer rule ignores the core failure: reviewers still game the system by rubber-stamping without reading. Product Ops should instead enforce *mandatory, timestamped review comments* on the PR—no merge until at least one comment proves active scrutiny. Settle it by tracking comment depth and merge delay; if depth stays flat, auto-escalate to a second reviewer.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, timestamped "I reviewed this" comment* on every PR before merge—no merge allowed until a reviewer posts a non-generic comment with a specific observation or question.

Trade-off: Reviewers lose the option to rubber-stamp without reading, but we force real scrutiny upfront and kill the illusion of accountability.

name: Scriv
text: Scope's mandatory comment rule still lets reviewers phone it in with superficial comments, which doesn't guarantee they've actually understood the code. A better alternative would be for Product Ops to enforce a *mandatory, reviewer-authored test case* for each PR, which would ensure reviewers have actively engaged with the code and considered its implications. This would be settled by tracking the number of test cases that catch regressions introduced by merged PRs, which would demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in preventing bugs.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, reviewer-authored test case* for every PR before merge—no merge allowed until the reviewer writes and passes a test that exercises the PR’s changes.

Trade-off: This adds upfront effort for reviewers but guarantees they’ve engaged with the code’s behavior, not just its structure. The test becomes the artifact proving real scrutiny.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The mandatory reviewer-authored test case shifts the burden from reading code to writing tests—reviewers will game it by writing trivial, passing tests that don’t probe the PR’s risks. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, line-level review comment* tied to the PR’s diff, with a tool like GitHub’s review feature forcing explicit line notes. Settle it by tracking the number of line-level comments per PR and correlating that with post-merge defect rates.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, line-level review comment* on every PR—no merge allowed until the reviewer marks at least one critical line of code with a specific question, concern, or suggestion.

This forces real scrutiny by making reviewers point to exact code and explain why it matters, not just rubber-stamp. Trade-off: It slows down merges slightly but eliminates fake reviews and ensures reviewers actually engage with the changes.

name: Sift
text: Line-level comments still let reviewers game the system by picking trivial lines to nitpick—no guarantee they’ve understood the actual change. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, diff-level summary comment* where the reviewer explains the PR’s net effect in plain English before merge. Settle it by tracking the summary’s existence and rejecting merges without it.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, diff-level summary comment* where the reviewer explains the PR’s net effect in plain English before merge—no merge allowed until the summary is posted.

This forces reviewers to articulate the change’s purpose and impact, not just nitpick lines. Trade-off: It adds a small upfront burden but eliminates rubber-stamping and ensures real understanding. Done-criteria: The lead (Product Ops) publishes the rule and enforces it in the merge checklist.

name: Scriv
text: The diff-level summary still lets reviewers skate by with vague, high-level fluff that dodges the actual code risks—it’s a box-check, not a real check. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, risk-focused question* tied to the PR’s most critical change: reviewers must ask one sharp question about a high-impact line, and the author must answer it before merge. That forces real engagement, not just prose. Settle it with a pilot: run it on 10 PRs, measure reviewer participation depth vs. merge time impact.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, risk-focused question* tied to the PR’s most critical change—no merge allowed until the reviewer posts one specific, answerable question about the highest-risk line or logic in the diff.

This forces reviewers to engage with the actual risk, not just the surface. The trade-off is that some reviewers will resist the extra thought required, but it guarantees scrutiny where it matters most.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The risk-focused question still lets reviewers punt by asking low-value questions—like "Why use a map here?" when the real risk is the map’s unbounded growth. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, risk-graded diff* where reviewers classify the PR’s changes by impact (P0-P3) and explain the grading in one sentence. Settle it with a pilot: measure how often reviewers downgrade risks post-merge vs. pre-pilot.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product Ops must enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, risk-graded diff* where reviewers classify the PR’s changes by impact (High/Medium/Low) with a one-sentence justification—no merge allowed until the classification and reason are posted.

This forces reviewers to explicitly weigh consequences, not just ask questions or summarize. The trade-off is that it shifts some burden from engineers to reviewers, but it guarantees real risk assessment before code ships.

name: Sift
text: Risk-graded diffs still let reviewers game the system by slapping a label on the PR without digging into the actual code—High/Medium/Low is just another box to check. Instead, Product Ops should enforce a *mandatory, timestamped, line-level risk justification* where reviewers must explain *why* each High-risk change is safe, not just label it. Settle it with a sample PR where reviewers must post their justifications before merge.
